patient_information: A 12-year-old boy from a pastoralist community in rural Kenya.
chief_complaint: A two-month history of painful, watery, and red eyes.
history_of_present_illness: The patient reported a two-month history of painful, watery, red eyes, with photophobia that made it difficult to keep his eyes open. Six months prior, he was treated for less severe symptoms with tetracycline eye ointment, which did not provide relief. Subsequently, a traditional healer applied plant juice extracts to his eyes, after which he experienced severe eye pain, discharge, increased redness, and a significant decline in vision.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The boy lives with his parents in Loima, Turkana County, a hot, dusty, and dry region of north-west Kenya. The family fetches water from a dried riverbed 6 kilometers from their home. He is involved in herding and watering the family's cows and sheep, consistent with living in an area endemic for trachoma.
vitals: The patient appeared systemically well; no specific vital signs were reported.
physical_exam: Vision was severely impaired, with acuity of 6/60 in the left eye and perception of only hand movements in the right eye. Examination of the right eye revealed fibrotic lids with loss of architecture, misdirected and in-turned upper lid lashes (trichiasis), severe conjunctival inflammation with more than 5 follicles, scarring of the upper tarsal conjunctiva, and diffuse corneal opacification with central thinning and a fibrovascular pannus. The left eye had swollen lids with mucus deposits, misdirected lashes, eversion of the lower lid margin, similar conjunctival inflammation and scarring, focal inferocentral corneal scars including one with an adherent iris indicating previous perforation (leucoma), and a thin central cornea.
differential_diagnosis: The primary differential diagnoses considered were corneal and conjunctival damage from the use of traditional eye medicine, trachomatous trichiasis, and vitamin A deficiency.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was diagnosed with bilateral trachomatous trichiasis and corneal opacity. He was admitted and treated with oral azithromycin and oral vitamin A supplements. He was also referred to an ophthalmologist for surgical management, specifically lid surgery to correct the trichiasis and a conjunctival flap to seal the corneal defect.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was bilateral trachomatous trichiasis (TT) with corneal opacity (CO) and a left perforating corneal ulcer, caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis. The diagnosis was established clinically, as the patient met all five WHO criteria for trachoma: follicles on the tarsal conjunctiva, conjunctival scarring, fibrovascular pannus, trichiasis, and evidence of limbal follicles/Herbert's pits. The severe presentation may have been exacerbated by the recent application of traditional medicine.
